news.author: Piero Cingari
news.content:
Every global recession of the past 50 years was preceded by the same economic warning signs.

Oil prices spiked. Central banks tightened. Asset prices boomed, money crowded into one hot sector and investors stopped pricing risk.

Today, those signals are back, according to Oxford Economics.

This time, elevated energy prices, rising bond yields and the artificial intelligence boom are playing the roles once held by Middle East oil shocks, Paul Volcker‘s rate hikes and the dot-com bubble.

“True, the full effects of the rise in energy prices and bond yields have yet to be felt,” Ben May, director of global macro research at Oxford Economics, said in emailed comments.

He added that only a further escalation in those pressures, or a sharp reversal of the AI boom, would push the world economy into recession.

There is a silver lining, however.

The current backdrop most closely resembles the run-up to 2001, the mildest of the six global recessions of the past half century.

Markets Are Already Testing the AI Signal

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) has fallen about 23% over the past month through Wednesday’s close.

That leaves it roughly 31% below its all-time high.

Several hyperscalers have cracked as well. Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is down nearly 16% in a month, while Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) have each lost about 13%.

Oxford Economics described the recent sharp drops in some hyperscaler shares as a warning shot.

Read Also: Tech Stocks Are Trading as If ChatGPT Never Happened, Data Shows

Meanwhile, the rest of the market has moved the other way.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP) gained 6.4% over the past month and closed Wednesday at an all-time high. The cap-weighted State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) slipped 0.4%.

In other words, the average S&P 500 stock has beaten the index by nearly seven percentage points in a month.

Bonds rallied, too.

The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:TLT) rose 6% over the month. The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 42 basis points to 4.89%, while the 30-year yield dropped about 39 basis points to 5.27%. The two-year yield eased about 22 basis points to 4.61%.

Oil, Rates and Risk Fill Out the Checklist

1. An oil shock. Before the 2001 recession, crude more than trebled in 18 months, according to Oxford Economics.

This year, Brent crude has climbed about 59% and traded near $97 a barrel Thursday morning. However, oil matters less to the global economy than it used to, May said.

2. Rising rates. Every prior global recession followed a tightening cycle.

This time, Oxford Economics is watching what borrowers actually pay rather than policy rates.

3 and 4. An asset price boom and overinvestment in one sector. The AI boom covers both. Above all, the U.S. now relies more on tech for growth than it did in 2000, according to the note.

5. Underpriced risk. Despite this year’s surge in bond yields, credit spreads have stayed narrow and stock gains have been strong. Consequently, bad news could trigger an abrupt repricing.

Read Also: From Tech Stocks to Staples: October Delivers Wall Street's Biggest Sector Rotation Since Dot-Com Bubble Burst

Why 2001 Fits Better Than 2008

The deepest downturns of the past five decades came with fiscal or financial crises, from Asia in 1997 to the eurozone and 2008.

That ingredient is missing today. Household and corporate debt in advanced economies has not exploded, and Oxford Economics is skeptical that a fiscal crisis is imminent.

The firm’s data show that advanced economies falling into recession in 2001-2002 lost less than 2% of output on average, peak to trough. In 2008-2009, the average loss was close to 6%.

“This trend of improving resilience may now be reversing, particularly because of the increasing frequency of supply shocks since the pandemic and the move towards more interventionist government policies,” May said.

Oxford Economics still expects global growth of 2.8% in 2027. The five signals describe a late-cycle economy that is more fragile than it looks, not a recession that has already started.

news.headline: Five Signals That Preceded Past Recessions Are Back — and AI Is at the Center
news.summary: Oxford Economics says five signals that preceded past recessions are back. Chip stocks sink 23% in a month as equal-weight stocks lead and bonds rally.

news.author: Daragh Thomas
news.content:
Big Tech has spent years pouring record sums into artificial intelligence. Now veteran strategist Ed Yardeni says hitting the brakes could be bullish.

“I’ve had the view that a slowing down in the AI build-out is actually a bullish story,” the Yardeni Research president told CNBC Thursday.

He was explaining a striking split in Wednesday’s post-midterm rally, when the Dow surged 1,569 points, its best day in more than 18 months. Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) gained 6.7% and Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) rose 6.1%, while Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) fell 3.2% and CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) sank 9.9%.

Why Spending Less Could Mean More Cash

Yardeni pointed to concerns that hyperscalers and smaller cloud providers have been building data centers and buying chips too quickly, “creating a lot of havoc,” without any guarantee of adequate returns.

Amazon illustrates the problem. The company generated $168.3 billion in operating cash flow over the past year, yet reported negative $42.4 billion in free cash flow as AI investment accelerated.

It expects approximately $220 billion in capital expenditures this year.

If hyperscalers slow their expansion, “their free cash flow will be less negative, maybe even turn positive,” Yardeni said.

Fewer new data centers would mean less cash going out the door, potentially improving returns on existing investments.

Political Speed Bumps

Texas could become a major obstacle to the AI build-out. Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s race Tuesday after promising to halt new data-center permits until lawmakers pass regulations.

Texas accounts for nearly 30% of planned U.S. data-center additions in 2028, SemiAnalysis estimates.

Politics isn’t the only obstacle. Yardeni also pointed to tighter financing, labor shortages and semiconductor constraints.

“I think these are all putting speed bumps in the AI build-out. And that’s a good thing,” he said.

He also welcomed the role of “bond vigilantes,” investors who demand higher returns for lending to risky borrowers, arguing that some “neo-clouds” shouldn’t be getting cheap credit.

But there’s a catch: Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta still plan more than $700 billion in capital investment this year. Slower construction could also constrain future revenue if AI demand keeps growing.

On Polymarket, traders see an 8% chance of an AI bubble bursting by December 31, rising to 23% by June 30, 2027. Yardeni’s argument points to a gentler path: a slower build-out that keeps overspending from turning into a full-blown downturn.

For now, Wall Street appears to be rewarding the prospect of spending discipline before Big Tech has started spending less.

U.S. stocks were mixed on Thursday, as the Dow Jones, S&P 500, and Nasdaq 100 index futures diverged, following Wednesday’s higher close.

U.S. nonfarm worker productivity grew by a robust 3.6% in the third quarter of 2026, successfully driving down unit labor costs as output outpaced a marginal increase in hours worked. Meanwhile, the labor market demonstrated ongoing resilience, with seasonally adjusted initial jobless claims for the week ending Oct. 31 dropping by 6,000 to a lower-than-expected 189,000.

Iran’s Security Chief Mohsen Rezaee said on Wednesday that Tehran had inflicted a political defeat on President Donald Trump, portraying the Republicans’ losses in the midterm elections as another consequence of Washington’s war with Iran. Axios reported on Wednesday that the U.S. military is wrapping up preparations for a potential return to major combat operations in Iran, including deploying additional military assets to the region.

Qatar is attempting to secure Washington and Tehran’s backing for a draft agreement that could prevent renewed fighting and potentially restart direct negotiations in the coming days.

Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury bond yielded 4.87%, and the 2-year Treasury bond yielded 4.58%, at the last check. The CME Group’s FedWatch tool projections show markets pricing in a 79.4% likelihood of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates after its December meeting.

Cues From Last Session

U.S. stocks closed higher on Wednesday, with consumer discretionary, financials, and communication services leading and energy, industrials, and information technology lagging. The Dow gained over 1500 points.

Insights From Analysts

CNBC host Jim Cramer said Wednesday that the post-election rally may not last as investors await the Labor Department’s employment data. He said election-driven trading could reverse when the nonfarm payrolls report arrives Friday, adding, “We could see a repeal of so much of this move that I hesitate to guess where we go next.” Cramer also said, “The elections did not upend the business cycle,” and urged investors to “never confuse” short-term stock moves for broader economic reality.

Jeff Buchbinder, LPL Financial chief equity strategist, said markets should focus on earnings, economic growth and AI investment after the midterms, adding that the S&P 500 has gained an average of 15.1% in the 12 months following midterm elections since 1950, with positive returns in all 19 periods.

He said the setup this cycle was not one for as much market volatility as in history, noting the average pre-midterms drawdown in the S&P 500 has been 17% and “this year we’ve gotten 9%.” Buchbinder also said divided government takes major sweeping tax and spending policies off the table and may imply less Treasury supply pressure and tempered rate volatility.

About 600,000 advanced H200 processors from Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) are reportedly awaiting shipment in Hong Kong amid Beijing’s import restrictions.

Nvidia chips remain stored in Hong Kong while mainland authorities withhold approval for large-scale deliveries, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the matter. China has permitted limited H200 shipments in recent months. Several major internet companies reportedly received about 10,000 chips each, while smaller volumes reached customers through intermediaries and indirect channels.

Beijing has not authorized broad imports into the mainland, despite demand from Chinese technology companies seeking more computing power for expanding AI operations.

By late October, an eight-card H200 server reportedly sold for more than 6 million yuan, or approximately $900,000. That price was roughly triple its level one year earlier. Servers containing Nvidia’s newer Blackwell chips reportedly sold for more than 20 million yuan or $2.99 million, although those products remain restricted under U.S. export controls.

Reuters reported last month that ByteDance, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (NYSE:BABA) and Tencent Holdings (OTC:TCEHY) had placed orders for more than 3 million Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards, an export-compliant but less powerful product, with a combined value exceeding $35 billion.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Read Also: Trump Labels Jensen Huang ‘Very Aboveboard’ Amid Chinese Spy Report Fallout, but Says It Is a ‘Very Complex Issue’

Nvidia’s H200 Becomes Trade Flashpoint

Nvidia’s H200 chip has become a focal point of broader U.S.-China trade and technology tensions. Washington initially banned H200 exports to China but later allowed sales to approved Chinese customers following trade negotiations between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Beijing has imposed its own restrictions on imports, citing concerns over dependence on U.S. technology.

Earlier this month, Nvidia has reportedly asked global data center partners to ensure at least 51% of their cloud-service revenue comes from non-Chinese customers, potentially restricting Chinese access to advanced AI computing infrastructure.

U.S. restrictions on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and semiconductor manufacturing equipment are limiting China’s ability to produce advanced AI chips. However, Futurum Equities strategist Shay Boloor told Benzinga that the curbs could also accelerate Beijing’s push to develop domestic alternatives by giving Chinese suppliers a larger captive market and stronger incentives to replace foreign technology.

Price Action: Year-to-date, Nvidia Stock climbed 7.31%, as per Benzinga Pro. The stock dropped 1.58% to $196.97 pre-market on Thursday.

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) could outperform Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) as AI investors shift from companies selling the hardware to those turning it into revenue, YouTube investor Joseph Carlson argues.

A day after Democrats swept Congress and data-center critics won key races, Amazon jumped 6.1% and Alphabet gained 3.2% Wednesday. Nvidia fell 3.2%, while Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) lost 7%.

Carlson, who shares his roughly $1.5 million stock portfolio with more than 500,000 YouTube subscribers, said it gained about $65,000 Wednesday, likely his biggest one-day gain ever. His Amazon stake alone added roughly $13,000.

Why Carlson Thinks the Winners Are Changing

Chip and memory makers have profited from extraordinary demand and shortages, but Carlson believes those bottlenecks will eventually ease.

In his view, Amazon, Google and Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) have something more durable: existing customers to whom they can sell AI services.

“To think that they’re not going to be able to monetize that many connections, I think is absurd,” Carlson said in a Wednesday video.

Carlson owns shares in all three companies. He also sees an upside to slowing data-center construction.

“The fact that this could be slowed down now isn’t bearish for big tech companies. In fact, this makes data centers more scarce,” he said.

Veteran strategist Ed Yardeni made a similar argument on CNBC Thursday, saying a slower AI buildout could actually be bullish for Big Tech by reducing capital spending and improving free cash flow.

Wall Street Joins the Rotation

Goldman Sachs’ trading desk reported a “clear rotation” into major cloud companies among hedge funds and traditional investment funds.

The bank’s technology specialists said Democratic victories could make new facilities harder to build, increasing the value of existing data centers with reliable power.

Amazon and Google could benefit twice from a slower AI buildout. They would spend less on new data centers while their existing computing capacity becomes more valuable.

AWS revenue grew 39% last quarter, while Google Cloud’s more than doubled.

That could be a very different story for Nvidia, which relies on continued demand for new chips. But with quarterly revenue more than doubling to $96.2 billion, there’s little evidence that demand has weakened yet.

On Polymarket, traders now give Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) roughly 60% odds of finishing 2026 as the world’s most valuable company, against 38% for Nvidia, on $9.6 million in trading volume.

Apple surged 5.3% to a record high Wednesday, overtaking Nvidia in market value. Unlike Amazon and Google, Apple has largely avoided massive AI infrastructure spending.
